title.en: Homage to the wrath and the weapons; Rudra asked to be gentle

summary: Fifteen ṛks. The worshipper salutes Rudra’s wrath, arrow, bow and arms, asks that his arrow, bow and body be auspicious (śiva) and not harm people or cattle, praises the red-brown Rudra who is seen even by cowherds and water-carriers, and ends by asking him to unstring his bow and lay his weapons away from us. Sāyaṇa reads every salutation as a plea that the weapon turn on the worshipper’s enemies and not on him.

vyakarana.note: The dative goes with namaḥ: ‘homage to X’ takes the dative (namaḥsvasti…, P. 2.3.16). So do iṣave, dhanvane, bāhubhyām.
The enclitic te (for tava, ‘your’; P. 8.1.22) never stands first in its clause; here it depends on manyave.
Imperative of as ‘to be’. In the first and third clauses the verb is understood; namaḥ is the subject: ‘homage be’.

translation.literal: Homage to your wrath, O Rudra, and also to your arrow homage. Homage be to your bow, and to your two arms homage.
translation.readable: O Rudra, homage to your wrath, and homage to your arrow; homage to your bow, and homage to your two arms.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa glosses manyu as anger (कोपः) and reads the salutation as a plea about where that anger should go: «स मन्युरस्मद्वैरिष्वेव प्रसरतु नत्वस्मासु» — may it spread among our enemies, not among us. The arrow, the bow and the arms that hold them are saluted in the same spirit: «न तु मयीत्यभिप्रायः», ‘the sense is: not against me’. The Kalpa he quotes uses these anuvākas for the Śatarudrīya offering at the building of the fire altar.
units.reflection: The hymn opens by bowing to the very things one fears — wrath, arrow, bow, arm — before asking for anything. Homage here is a way of facing what threatens.

vyakarana.note: śiva + the superlative suffix -tama (P. 5.3.55), feminine to agree with iṣuḥ.
Perfect of bhū. With śivam … dhanuḥ: ‘your bow has become kindly’ — said as an appeal that it be so.
Picks up all three: the arrow, the bow and the quiver (Sāyaṇa takes tayā with each).

translation.literal: Your arrow which is most kindly, your bow which has become kindly, your missile which is kindly — with that, O Rudra, be gracious to us.
translation.readable: O Rudra, with your arrow made most kindly, your bow made kindly and your quiver made kindly, be gracious to us.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa reads śiva here as शान्त, calm or appeased: the arrow is शान्ततमा, the bow शान्तं. He takes śaravyā as the quiver (तवेषुधिः) and mṛḍaya as सुखय, ‘make happy’. Their calm, he says, is because they do not move against devotees: «भक्तेषु प्रवृत्त्यभावात्तेषां शान्तत्वम्».

flags.note: śaravyā is ‘missile, arrow-shot’ in the dictionaries; Sāyaṇa takes it as the quiver. The translation follows Sāyaṇa and the word table gives both.

samasa.vigraha: गिरौ स्थित्वा शं तनोति इति गिरिशन्तः
samasa.meaning: (Sāyaṇa) he who, staying on the mountain, spreads weal — śam with -ta from tan ‘to spread’; MW takes it as = giriśa, ‘inhabiting mountains’

vyakarana.note: Instrumental sg. of tanū ‘body’, with the Vedic uv for v (tanuvā = classical tanvā).
From śam ‘weal’ with the superlative suffix -tama: ‘most beneficent’. Instr. sg. f., agreeing with tanuvā; a derivative, not a compound.
Feminine in -inī of -kāśin ‘appearing, showing’, from kāś ‘to appear, shine’, with the negative a-.

Intensive of kāś ‘to shine, be visible’ (reduplicated stem cākaś-, with the connecting ī of the intensive), imperative 2nd sg. in -hi. The preverb abhi ‘towards’ carries the accent and is written apart in the text; it is kept on its verb, as the brief and Sāyaṇa write it.
Nom. sg. of the ū-stem tanū. Before the vowel of aghorā its visarga appears as r.

translation.literal: O Rudra, your body which is kindly, not dreadful, not of evil aspect — with that most beneficent body, O Giriśanta, look upon us.
translation.readable: O Rudra, your kindly body, not dreadful, showing no evil — with that most gracious body, Giriśanta, look upon us.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa begins from the teaching that Rudra has two bodies, «द्वे हि रुद्रस्य तनू», and cites a passage he says is taught later in the text: «रुद्रो वा एष यदग्निस्तस्यैते तनुवौ घोराऽन्या शिवाऽन्या» — this Agni is Rudra; of his two bodies one is dreadful, the other kindly. The dreadful one harms, the kindly one favours: «हिंसिका घोराऽनुग्राहिका शिवा». He explains apāpakāśinī through its opposite, «पाप हिंसारूपमनिष्टं काशयतीति पापकाशिनी» — the body that does not bring to light evil in the form of harm — and giriśanta as the one who, staying on the mountain Kailāsa, always spreads happiness to living beings: «गिरौ कैलासे स्थित्वा नित्यं प्राणिभ्यो यः शं सुखं तनोति स गिरिशंतः». Abhicākaśīhi is to shine forth looking towards the worshipper («मामभिलक्ष्य»): by showing this body, make me happy.
units.reflection: The prayer does not ask for a different god but for the other body of the same one, and asks only that it look.

flags.note: Sāyaṇa reads aghorā and apāpakāśinī as two words (अघोरा … अपापकाशिनी), and the accents appear to mark an udātta on the initial a- of each (त॒नूरघो॒रापा॑पकाशिनी: the syllables र and रा are both unmarked, i.e. udātta, so the stretch has two udāttas, not the one of a single compound). The DCS annotation of TS 4.5.1 takes aghorāpāpakāśinī as one compound. Kept as two words.

apāpakāśinī: MW ‘not ill-looking’ (kāś ‘to appear’); Sāyaṇa ‘not bringing harm to light’. giriśanta: MW gives it as = giriśa, ‘inhabiting mountains’; Sāyaṇa derives it from śam + tan, ‘spreading happiness from the mountain’. The word table gives both.

vyakarana.note: Vedic infinitive in -tave from as ‘to throw’ (4th class, asyati), a dative of purpose: ‘to shoot’.
Present of bhṛ, 3rd class, reduplicated bi-bhar-: ‘you hold’. Before astave its i becomes y. The pañcāśat mark [1] stands between haste and bibharṣi; no sandhi is made across it.
Unaugmented iṣ-aorist (injunctive) of hiṃs, with the prohibitive mā: ‘do not harm’. After mā the augment is not used (na māṅyoge, P. 6.4.74).
Present participle of gam (reduplicated ja-gat), used as a neuter noun: ‘that which moves’.
giri + -tra from trā ‘to protect’, the ā dropped before the suffix: ‘protector of the mountain’.

translation.literal: The arrow which, O Giriśanta, you hold in [your] hand to shoot — make that kindly, O Giritra; do not harm man [or] the moving world.
translation.readable: Giriśanta, the arrow you hold in your hand to shoot — make it kindly, protector of the mountain; harm neither man nor anything that moves.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa takes astave as ‘to hurl at enemies’ («अस्तवे वैरिषु प्रक्षेप्तुं») and giritra as the one who protects the mountain called Kailāsa («कैलासाख्यं गिरिं त्रायते पालयतीति गिरित्रः»). The arrow is to be made calm towards us. Puruṣa is our man («पुरुषमस्मदीयं मनुष्यं»), and jagat everything that moves apart from men, such as cattle («जङ्गमं गवादिकं»).

flags.note: The DCS annotation tags mā here as the pronoun (mad, acc. sg.). With the augmentless aorist hiṃsīḥ it is the prohibitive particle mā, and Sāyaṇa reads «मा हिंसीः» so. The edition keeps the particle.

Its initial a- has already merged with giriśa (giriśa + accha → giriśāccha), so the surface given for it is -ācchā.

samasa.meaning: who lies (dwells) on the mountain (śī ‘to lie’)
having no sickness; free from disease
of good mind, glad

vyakarana.note: Present 1st pl. with the Vedic ending -masi (classical vadāmaḥ). Unaccented, as a finite verb in a main clause.
Adverb/preverb ‘towards’, construed with the accusative tvā: accha vad ‘to call to, address’. Written apart from the verb (brief rule 3). Pada form accha; acchā in the Saṃhitā.
Enclitic acc. sg. of yuṣmad (tvāmau dvitīyāyāḥ, P. 8.1.23).
Subjunctive of as, 3rd sg. (as-a-t), after yathā ‘so that’: ‘may be’.

Nom. sg. of the bahuvrīhi sumanas in its masculine/feminine form (-āḥ, which before asat loses its visarga). A neuter agreeing with jagat would be sumanaḥ (joining as *sumano ’sat). Sāyaṇa refers it to the world.
Vedic emphatic particle: sarvam it jagat ‘the whole world, every part of it’.

translation.literal: With kindly speech, O Giriśa, we call towards you, so that our whole world, all of it, may be free from disease [and] well-minded.
translation.readable: Giriśa, we call to you with words of good omen, that all our world may be free from sickness and glad at heart.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa derives giriśa from the one who lies, that is abides, on the mountain Kailāsa («शेते»). He reads accha as ‘to reach [you]’ («त्वामच्छ प्राप्तुं») and the speech as kindly speech in the form of praise («शिवेन मङ्गलेन स्तुतिरूपेण वचसा»); vadāmasi is ‘we pray’ («वदामसि वयं प्रार्थयामहे»). The world is every moving creature, men, cattle and the rest, and the wish is that it be free from disease, «रोगरहितं», and «सौमनस्योपेतं», glad of mind; he completes the sentence with «तथा कुरु», ‘so act’.

flags.note: sumanāḥ is a masculine/feminine nom. sg. (the neuter would be sumanaḥ, joining as *sumano ’sat), yet the subject in the sentence is the neuter jagat. Sāyaṇa refers it to the world (सौमनस्योपेतं); DCS tags it masculine. The translation follows Sāyaṇa; the agreement is not explained here.
DCS reads one verb, acchāvadāmasi. The text writes acchā apart from the unaccented verb, and Sāyaṇa glosses accha by itself (त्वामच्छ प्राप्तुं), so accha is its own word here.
naḥ: DCS tags it dative (‘for us’); Sāyaṇa takes it as genitive with jagat (‘our world’), followed here.

samasa.vigraha: यातूनि दधाति इति यातुधानः, स्त्रियां यातुधानी
samasa.meaning: one who holds sorcery: a sorcerer, a demon (here feminine)

vyakarana.note: adhi + avocat. avocat is the reduplicated aorist of vac (a-va-uc-a-t), 3rd sg. The preverb adhi carries the accent (ádhy avocat) and is written joined, so it is kept on its verb. Sāyaṇa reads the past form as a wish (वदतु).
Agent noun in -tṛ from vac with adhi: ‘one who speaks for’ (MW: advocate, protector, comforter).
Present participle of the causative jambhaya- (root jambh ‘snap at, crush’), nom. sg. m., agreeing with the subject of avocat. Its objects are ahīn and yātudhānyaḥ.
Plural of yātudhānī; with sarvāḥ it is the object of jambhayan, so accusative — an acc. pl. in -yaḥ beside the -īḥ of classical devī-stems (DCS also tags it acc. pl.).
Acc. pl. m. of ahi ‘snake’. Before ca its -īn appears as -īm̐ś.

translation.literal: The advocate has spoken for [us], the first, the divine physician, crushing all the snakes and all the sorceresses.
translation.readable: He has spoken for us, the advocate, the first, the divine healer, crushing every snake and every sorceress.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa reads adhyavocat as a wish: «अतस्तादृशो रुद्रोऽध्यवोचन्मां सर्वाधिकं वदतु» — may such a Rudra speak of me as foremost, for once he has said it, it is established. Prathama is «देवानां मध्ये मुख्यो», chief among the gods; daivya is the one worthy of all the gods («सर्वान्देवानर्हति»), able himself to protect them; and he is a physician because the mere thought of him quiets every disease («ध्यानमात्रेण सर्वरोगोपशमनादयं चिकित्सकः»). Jambhayan is «विनाशयन्», destroying, and the yātudhānīs are «राक्षसजातीः», the kinds of rākṣasa.

flags.note: adhyavocat is an aorist, ‘has spoken for’; Sāyaṇa takes it as a wish (वदतु, ‘may he speak’). Both translations keep the tense of the Sanskrit.
yātudhānyaḥ is taken as acc. pl. f. (object of jambhayan, with sarvāḥ), as DCS also tags it; the ending -yaḥ, where -īḥ is the expected accusative of such a stem, is not explained here.

samasa.meaning: very auspicious

vyakarana.note: Nom. sg. m. of adas, the pronoun of what is further off: ‘that one there’.
Acc. sg. f. of idam, governed by abhitaḥ ‘around’. Sāyaṇa supplies ‘this earth’ (bhūmi, f.).
Past participle of śri ‘to resort to, rest on’, nom. pl. m., with ye … rudrāḥ.
Preverb of īmahe, separated from it by eṣām heḍaḥ (tmesis): ava … īmahe ‘we deprecate, we appease’ (MW: ‘to beg pardon for, conciliate’).
1st pl. ātmanepada. MW lists -īmahe with ava under i, as an intensive form; unaccented as the finite verb of the main clause.
Acc. sg. of the neuter s-stem heḍas ‘anger’ (pausal heḍaḥ, heḍa before the vowel of īmahe).
Adverb with the suffix -śas: ‘by thousands’.

translation.literal: That one who is copper-red, ruddy, and also tawny, very auspicious — and the Rudras who, by thousands, abide in the quarters around this [earth]: their anger we deprecate.
translation.readable: He who is copper-red, ruddy and tawny, wholly auspicious, and the Rudras who abide in their thousands in every quarter around this earth — we pray their anger away.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa identifies the one described as the sun in its orb («मण्डलस्थादित्यरूपः»): copper-red at rising («उदयकालेऽत्यन्तरक्तः»), ruddy after it, tawny («पिङ्गलः») higher still; the other colours of the day are to be inferred the same way. He is sumaṅgala because he dispels darkness. The other Rudras are his rays («रश्मिरूपा रुद्राः»), set in the quarters around this earth («इमामभितोऽस्या भूमेः परितो»), in their thousands. Their heḍaḥ is a sharpness like anger, which we ward off by devotion, salutation and the like: «हेडः क्रोधसदृशं तीक्ष्णत्वमवेमहे भक्तिनमस्कारादिना निवारयामः».

flags.note: imām: Sāyaṇa reads इमाम्, ‘this [earth]’ (इमामभितोऽस्या भूमेः), governed by abhitaḥ, and DCS has imām (acc. sg. f.). The brief’s illustration of vowel fusion cites this place as च इमान्. The spelling चेमाँ रुद्राः fits either (m before r is written ँ, and so is -ān before r); the edition follows Sāyaṇa.
īmahe: MW lists it (with ava) as an intensive form of i; DCS lemmatises it under ī. The sense with ava, ‘we deprecate, appease [anger]’, is secure; the formation is not settled here.

translation.literal: That one who glides down, blue-necked, deep red — and the cowherds have seen him, the women who carry water have seen [him], and all beings [have seen] him — he, seen, will be gracious to us.
translation.readable: He who glides down, blue-necked and deep red — the cowherds have seen him, the women carrying water have seen him, all creatures have seen him: seen, may he be gracious to us.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa again takes Rudra as the sun. He is nīlagrīva from holding the Kālakūṭa poison («कालकूटविषधारणेन नीलवर्णा ग्रीवा यस्यासौ नीलग्रीवः»), vilohita as especially red («विशेषेण लोहितवर्णः»), and his gliding down is the course he follows to bring about its rising and setting («संपादयितुं प्रवर्तते»). The cowherds are those without the training of the Veda and śāstra («गोपा वेदशास्त्रसंस्काररहिता गोपाला»), the udahāryaḥ are women who carry water («उदकानां हारिण्यो योषितः»), and all beings are cows, buffaloes and the rest. This is why Rudra takes the sun’s form: «सर्वेषां दर्शनार्थमेव हि रुद्रस्याऽऽदित्यमूर्तिधारणम्», that all may see him; his form on Kailāsa «वेदशास्त्राभिज्ञैरेव दृश्यते नान्यैः», is seen only by those versed in the Veda and śāstra. Mṛḍayāti he reads as a wish: may he make us happy.
units.reflection: The verse insists on who has seen him — the cowherd, the woman carrying water — before it asks anything of him.

flags.note: naḥ: Sāyaṇa takes it as the object (नोऽस्मान्, ‘us’), as with mṛḍaya in ṛk 2; DCS tags it dative. The edition follows Sāyaṇa.

translation.readable: Homage to the blue-necked one, the thousand-eyed, the bountiful; and to his followers too I have paid homage.

units.traditional: For Sāyaṇa the blue-necked one of the last ṛk now takes further forms: thousand-eyed as Indra («स एवेन्द्रमूर्तिधारणेन सहस्राक्षः»), and mīḍhvas as Parjanya, the pourer of rain («पर्जन्य-मूर्ति-धारणेन», «सेचको वृष्टिकर्तेत्यर्थः»). The satvans are living beings in the role of his servants («भृत्यरूपाः प्राणिनः»), and the worshipper says he has paid homage to all of them.

translation.readable: Loosen the string at both ends of your bow, and the arrows in your hand, Lord, cast them away.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa glosses bhagavaḥ as «भगवन् पूजावन् महद्-ऐश्वर्य-संपन्न» — worshipful, possessed of great lordship. Rudra is asked to take down the bowstring that rests at both tips of his bow («उभयोर् आर्त्नियोः कोट्योर् अवस्थितां ज्यां मौर्वीं», pramuñca being «प्रमुञ्चावरोपय») and to throw away the arrows in his hand («परावप परित्यज»).

vyakarana.note: Gerund of tan ‘to stretch’ with ava ‘down’: ‘having let [the bow] down’, that is, unstrung it. Compounded with a preverb the gerund takes -ya (samāse ’nañpūrve ktvo lyap, P. 7.1.37); the root’s n is lost and t is added before -ya (ava-ta-t-ya).
Gerund in -ya of śṝ ‘to crush, break’ with ni ‘down’; the ṝ becomes īr (ni-śīr-ya).
Vedic acc. pl. n. in -ā (classical mukhāni): ‘the points’ of the arrowheads.
Voc. sg. of the bahuvrīhi śateṣudhi; iṣudhi ‘quiver’ (MW).
Enclitic dat. (or gen.) pl. of asmad with śivaḥ … sumanāḥ: ‘kindly to us’.

translation.literal: Having unstrung [your] bow, you, O thousand-eyed one, O you of a hundred quivers, having broken off the points of the arrowheads, be kindly [and] well-minded to us.
translation.readable: Unstring your bow, thousand-eyed one with a hundred quivers; break off the points of your arrowheads, and be kind and gracious to us.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa takes sahasrākṣa as having a thousand eyes in the form of Indra («इन्द्ररूपेण»), and śateṣudhi as the one whose quivers, the sheaths that hold the arrows, number a hundred («शतसंख्याका इषुधयो बाणस्थापनकोशा यस्यासौ शतेषुधिः»). Avatatya means having taken the string off the bow, and niśīrya having made the points of the arrowheads crumble downward into the quivers («न्यग्भावेन शीर्णानि कृत्वा»). So disarmed, Rudra is asked to be calm and favourable towards us: «सुमना अनुग्रहयुक्तः सञ्शिवः शान्तो भव».

flags.note: niśīrya: from śṝ ‘to crush, break’ with ni; Sāyaṇa understands the arrowheads as made to crumble downward into the quivers. The translation gives the plain sense, ‘having broken off’.

vyakarana.note: Bahuvrīhi vi + jyā, the ā shortened in the compound adjective (vijya-), neuter to agree with dhanuḥ. ‘Be’ is understood; Sāyaṇa supplies अस्तु.
Gen. sg. of kapardin ‘wearing the kaparda, braided and knotted hair’ (MW): ‘the bow of Kapardin’.
bāṇa + the possessive suffix -vat: ‘having arrows’. MW and Sāyaṇa both take it as the quiver.
Aorist of naś ‘to be lost, perish’ (MW: aneśat), 3rd pl.; its final n is doubled before asya.
MW: ābhu ‘empty, void’. Sāyaṇa’s comment on it is damaged in the printed bhāṣya; he takes it as limited capacity: able to hold the arrows, not to let them be drawn.
A rare word. Sāyaṇa: the holder of the arrows (बाणाधारः), or that which can draw the sword. MW (from the lexicons) gives ‘embracing; a bowman; the shoulder’.

translation.literal: Stringless [be] the bow of Kapardin, and the arrow-holder without arrowheads; his arrows have vanished; empty [is] his niṣaṅgathi.
translation.readable: Stringless the bow of the one with braided hair, and his quiver without arrowheads; his arrows are gone, his sheath is empty.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa supplies ‘be’ (astu) throughout: «विगतज्याकमस्तु», may the bow be stringless. Kapardin is «कपर्दो जटाजूटः सोऽस्यास्तीति कपर्दी», the one whose kaparda is the knot of matted hair. Bāṇavān is the quiver, so called because the arrows stay in it («बाणा अस्मिंस्तिष्ठन्तीति बाणवान् इषुधिः»), and it is to be viśalya in the sense that no arrowhead shows outside it, the heads being kept within. Aneśan he takes as a wish: the arrows, put away in the quiver, «वेद्धुम् असमर्था भवन्तु», may be unable to pierce. The niṣaṅgathi, the holder of the arrows («निषङ्गथिर् बाणाधार»), is to be ābhu: able only to hold them (the printed bhāṣya is damaged here), «न तु बाणाकर्षण-योग्य इत्यर्थः», not fit for the arrows to be drawn. As an alternative he takes niṣaṅgathi as that which can draw the sword («अथवा निषङ्गथिः खड्गाकर्षण-समर्थः»).

flags.note: niṣaṅgathi is rare and its sense is not secure. Sāyaṇa: arrow-holder (बाणाधारः), or that which can draw the sword; MW, from the lexicons: ‘embracing, an embrace; a bowman; a charioteer; the shoulder’. The translation leaves the word as niṣaṅgathi in the literal and gives ‘sheath’ in the readable.
ābhuḥ: MW ‘empty, void’; Sāyaṇa, in a damaged passage, takes it as having power only to hold the arrows. The translation gives ‘empty’.
aneśan is an aorist, ‘have perished, vanished’; Sāyaṇa reads it as a wish (असमर्था भवन्तु, ‘may they be unable [to pierce]’). The translations keep the tense.

vyakarana.note: Superlative in -tama of mīḍhvas, built on the weak stem mīḍhuṣ- (ṣ + t → ṣṭ): ‘most bountiful’, vocative.
Feminine noun from hi ‘to impel’ (MW): ‘missile, weapon’.
Perfect of bhū. Sāyaṇa takes yā te hetiḥ and haste babhūva te dhanuḥ as two clauses: the weapon that is yours, and the bow that has been in your hand.
pari … bhuja, the preverb written apart: imperative of bhuj ‘to bend’ (6th class, bhujati), with pari ‘to bend around, encompass’ (MW). The text’s ब्भ is the doubling of recitation.
Instr. sg. f. of ayakṣma ‘without sickness, causing no harm’, agreeing with tayā (the heti; Sāyaṇa extends it to the bow).
Adverb in -tas from viśva: ‘from all sides’.

translation.literal: The missile which is yours, O most bountiful, [and] the bow [which] has been in your hand — with that, harmless, you, encompass us on all sides.
translation.readable: Most bountiful one, with the weapon that is yours and the bow that has been in your hand, made harmless, shelter us on every side.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa reads mīḍhuṣṭama as bountiful in the highest degree, the greatest giver of what is wished. The heti is any weapon of his, such as the sword («खड्गादिरूपं यदायुधं»), and beside it stands the bow that has been in his hand. With these, made «अयक्ष्मयाऽनुपद्रवकारिण्या», causing no harm, Rudra is asked: «परिभुज सर्वतः परिपालय», protect us on every side.

flags.note: corrections.json, N1.13 (orthographic): W1 writes परि॑ ब्भुज, the doubled bh of the Taittirīya recitation; W2 a single bh. The word is bhuja either way; the junction is declared as recitational doubling.

Both witnesses spell the instrumental अ॑यक्ष॒मया॒ (ayakṣamayā), which is not a word. The word is ayakṣmayā: Sāyaṇa «अयक्ष्मयाऽनुपद्रवकारिण्या», DCS ayakṣmayā, and the same stem as अय॒क्ष्मँ in ṛk 5. The accent mark written after क्ष looks like the anudātta of य॒ (a-ya-kṣmá-yā) displaced, with the virāma of ष् lost (Unicode क्ष + ॒ + म). The padaccheda gives अयक्ष्मया; text.json is not changed, so the editor should log a correction (proposed: अ॑य॒क्ष्मया॒) before this unit can rejoin.

atho = atha u, ‘and also’, as in ṛk 9.

translation.literal: May the missile of your bow avoid us on all sides; and also the quiver which [is] yours — set it down far from us.
translation.readable: May the missile of your bow pass us by on every side, and the quiver that is yours, lay it down far from us.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa takes the missile of the bow as arrow and arrowhead («बाणशल्यरूपा»), and parivṛṇaktu as «परिवृणक्तु वर्जितान्करोतु, मा बाधतामित्यर्थः» — let it leave us aside, that is, not afflict us. The quiver is to be set down away from us (he glosses āre asmat as ‘far from us’), nidhehi being «निधेहि स्थापय». With this ṛk his commentary on the first anuvāka ends.
units.reflection: The anuvāka ends where it began, with the bow, but now the request is simply distance: lay it down away from us.
